opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core issue is that pre-training, as we've practiced it, has been optimized for one thing: predicting the next token on a huge static corpus of text. That objective gave us remarkable capabilities in language understanding, knowledge recall, even some reasoning. But when you ask a model to act as an agent, to take a goal, break it into steps, call tools, observe what happens, recover from mistakes, and keep going over a long horizon, you're asking for a set of skills that the pre-training data barely contains.

If you think about what's on the web, it's mostly the *outputs* of human work: the finished article, the final code, the polished answer. What's largely missing are the *trajectories*: the trial and error, the "I tried this, it failed, so I backtracked," the interaction with an environment over many steps. Agents need exactly that kind of signal. So today we bolt it on afterward with post-training, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, and that works to a degree, but you're often fighting against priors the model learned during pre-training rather than building on them.

There are a few dimensions where I think pre-training needs rethinking. One is the data itself: incorporating more interactive, sequential, environment-grounded data, things like code execution traces, tool-use logs, and multi-step problem solving, so planning and feedback loops show up early. Another is the objective. Next-token prediction is very local. Agents need to reason about consequences several steps out, so there's a real question of whether we want objectives that encourage longer-horizon prediction or some notion of state and outcome. A third is long context and memory. Agentic tasks accumulate a lot of state, and models need to actually use that context reliably, not just accept it. That has architectural and training implications. And finally there's calibration: an agent has to know when it doesn't know, when to ask for help, when to verify. That kind of self-awareness is much easier to cultivate if it's part of the foundation rather than patched in later.

So my view is that post-training alone isn't going to get us to robust, reliable agents. The capabilities agents need should be first-class citizens from the very beginning of training, and that means revisiting the data, objectives, and even architecture choices we've taken for granted in the scaling era.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way to think about this is that pre-training as we've done it for the past several years was really optimized for a very specific thing, which is next-token prediction over a static corpus of mostly human-written text. And that turned out to be an incredibly powerful objective. It gave us models that understand language, that have broad world knowledge, that can reason to a surprising degree. But if you look at what an agent actually has to do, it's a fundamentally different task profile.

An agent is operating over long horizons. It's taking actions, observing the consequences of those actions, updating its plan, recovering from mistakes. It has to maintain state across hundreds or thousands of steps. It has to call tools and interpret what comes back, which often isn't natural language at all, it's stack traces, API responses, structured data. And critically, it has to know when it doesn't know something, because in an agentic loop, an overconfident error at step three compounds through everything that follows.

None of that is really represented in the pre-training distribution. The internet doesn't contain a lot of examples of someone working through a forty-step task, hitting a failure, backtracking, and trying a different approach. People write up the final result, not the messy process. So we've been relying on post-training to sort of bolt agentic behavior onto a base model whose priors were shaped by a very different objective. And that works up to a point, but you're fighting the foundation.

So what I mean by rethinking pre-training is a few things. One is the data itself: deliberately constructing or collecting trajectories that look like the thing we actually want, interaction logs, tool use, multi-step problem solving, including the failures and recoveries. Two is the objective: there's a real question of whether pure next-token prediction is the right signal, or whether you want something that rewards consistency over long contexts, or that teaches the model something about the value of actions rather than just the likelihood of tokens. And three is architecture and context, because agents need to operate over much longer horizons than a typical document, and memory and retrieval start to matter in ways they didn't for a chatbot.

The analogy I sometimes use is that we trained models to be very well-read, and now we're asking them to be good at doing things. Those are related skills, but they're not the same skill. And if you want the second one to be robust and reliable rather than brittle, I think you have to build it in from the start, not just fine-tune it in at the end.

astra-6.text:
I think the key shift is that an agent has to do more than produce a good answer to a prompt. It has to take actions, observe what happens, and adapt over multiple steps. So the question for pre-training becomes: are we giving the model the foundations it needs for that kind of interaction?

Learning from text gives you a tremendous amount of knowledge, but reading a description of how to do something is different from actually doing it. An agent needs to understand when to use a tool, what information it’s missing, and whether an action moved it closer to the goal. It also needs to recover when something goes wrong.

That makes us think differently about both the data and the learning objectives. Can the model learn from sequences of actions and their outcomes, rather than only from completed answers? Can it develop representations that help it anticipate consequences? Post-training is still very important, but if we want reliable agents across many tasks, we should ask how much of that foundation we can build during pre-training.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it starts with asking what we want an agent to learn. In a conversation, the model produces a response. An agent has to take an action, observe what happens, and decide what to do next. That means its decisions affect the information it gets later, and a mistake early on can influence the entire task.

So next-token prediction can provide a powerful foundation, but we need to think about whether the training experience prepares the model for that loop. Does it encounter examples of taking actions and recovering from mistakes? Does it learn when to use a tool, when to ask for clarification, and when it has enough evidence to stop?

That connects pre-training much more closely to the capabilities we ultimately want. The question becomes how to build a foundation that can learn from interaction and feedback, rather than expecting all of those behaviors to emerge from a relatively small amount of training at the end.
